value.overview: The Blue-vented Hummingbird (Saucerottia hoffmanni) is a small hummingbird of Central America, occurring mainly in western Nicaragua and Costa Rica. It is a member of the emerald hummingbirds and is often associated with relatively dry, open or semi-open habitats. The species has a generally dark green appearance, a dusky throat, and blue coloration on the rump, lower back, and tail. It may visit gardens and other human-modified areas where flowering plants are available.
value.classification: The Blue-vented Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the emerald group, tribe Trochilini. It was formerly treated as a subspecies of the Steely-vented Hummingbird, but many modern taxonomic treatments recognize Saucerottia hoffmanni as a separate species.
value.identification: This is a small, relatively subdued emerald hummingbird with dark green upperparts and underparts, a dusky grayish throat, and blue to blue-green coloration concentrated on the rump, lower back, and tail. The plumage may appear less brightly metallic than that of several related hummingbirds. Its straight, slender bill and rapid wingbeats are typical of hummingbirds. Identification is most reliable when the blue tail and rump, darker throat, and preference for open habitats are considered together.
value.rangeHabitat: The Blue-vented Hummingbird ranges from southern or western Nicaragua south through much of Costa Rica, making Costa Rica an important part of its limited Central American range. In Costa Rica it occurs especially on the Pacific slope and in the central interior, including dry and seasonally dry regions, while records also occur in other suitable areas. It uses scrub, savanna, forest edges, secondary woodland, plantations, gardens, and other semi-open habitats, generally from sea level to about 1,800 meters.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local or seasonal movements, apparently following flowering resources and shifting between drier habitats and moister areas during the dry season.
value.breeding: Detailed information on breeding remains limited. The breeding season appears to extend at least from December through April, including records from Costa Rica. The nest is a small cup made from plant down and spider web, with lichens attached to the outside for camouflage. Reported nests have been placed on slender branches, including a dead Cecropia branch and a Ficus vine. As in other hummingbirds, the female is expected to provide most or all nest care.
value.dietFeeding: The Blue-vented Hummingbird feeds mainly on nectar from a wide variety of flowering vines, shrubs, and trees. It often forages at the height of small trees and may defend productive feeding territories. It also captures small insects, usually in short aerial sallies and sometimes from surfaces near water. In Costa Rica, gardens and secondary habitats can provide useful feeding opportunities when native or ornamental plants are flowering.
value.behavior: This hummingbird is active and agile, moving quickly between flowers and perches. It commonly forages in open vegetation, woodland edges, scrub, and gardens, and may aggressively defend nectar sources from other hummingbirds. Its movements are usually local, but individuals can shift location as flowering conditions change. Calls include sharp, high notes, while the song has been described as a repeated buzzy or squeaky phrase.

conservation.populationTrend: A reliable separate global population trend for Saucerottia hoffmanni is not available. The species remains locally encountered across suitable habitat in Costa Rica and Nicaragua, but its restricted range means that regional habitat changes should be monitored.
